title: California v. Mullin - Cato Institute
content: Our brief argues that the $100,000 fee on entry is an unconstitutional tax imposed without congressional authority. Just as the Supreme Court held in striking down the “Liberation Day” tariffs that the power to “regulate” is not the power to tax, the statutory power to “restrict” entry does not authorize the president to charge for it. Learn more about Cato’s Amicus Briefs Program. The Trump administration has attempted to impose a $100,000 fee on applications for H‑1B visas, which are used by tech firms, research institutions, and other organizations to hire immigrant workers and researchers with various specialized skills. A group of states sued to challenge the fee, and a federal district court invalidated the $100,000 fee on the grounds that the executive had illegally usurped Congress’s power to impose taxes. Now the case is at the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, and Cato and Professor Ilya Somin have filed an amicus brief supporting the states (with thanks to Michael McConnell, Phillip Wilkinson, and Deno Himonas of Wilson Sonsini for drafting the brief). Our brief explains why the fee is an unconstitutional tax imposed without congressional authority. The tax power was, as Alexander Hamilton explained, “the most important of the authorities proposed to be conferred upon the Union.” As the Supreme Court held in striking down the “Liberation Day” tariffs, the power to “regulate” is not the power to tax and Congress did not clearly delegate its taxing power in the IEEPA statute. This case asks whether the same president—by imposing a tax of his own devising on the entry of noncitizens and calling it a “restriction” on entry—may accomplish by a different label what the Supreme Court’s holding forbade. The exaction here is a tax because its defining feature is to raise revenue. It is neither a fee contributing to the costs of operating the program nor a penalty. And the statutory power to “restrict” entry is not the power to “tax” entry. Even if the government has the power to limit or qualify entry, that says nothing about the power to charge for the privilege of entry. And the Government can identify no statute in which the words “restrict” or “restriction” confer tax authority. In addition, the government’s interpretation of the relevant statutes violates the major questions doctrine, which requires Congress to speak clearly when delegating power over a major economic or political issue to the executive. The power to impose unlimited taxes on any visa holders or immigrants entering into the United States is undoubtedly a major one. If, nonetheless, the court concludes that Congress did somehow grant the government the sweeping power it claims, it would violate the constitutional nondelegation doctrine, which constrains delegations of legislative power to the executive. The First Circuit should affirm the district court and hold the $100,000 fee to be an unauthorized and illegal tax. Professor of Law, George Mason University, and B. Kenneth Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies, Cato Institute Director, Robert A. title: V-Beyond Brings 31 Vietnamese Artists to Anaheim’s Honda Center in Landmark V-Pop Showcase - buzzmusic
content: Vietnamese pop music is taking its ambitions global with V-Beyond, a landmark arena concert at Anaheim’s Honda Center featuring 31 artists across multiple generations of V-pop, including Thai VG, Hà An Huy, and UPRIZE. Organized by YeaH1 Group in a strategic alliance with iMe Entertainment, Sony Music, and AlphaZ, the festival-scale production represents a significant step in bringing contemporary Vietnamese music to North American audiences. Under the theme “Road to V-BEYOND | Vietnamese Soul. America’s Stage,” the showcase brings together established performers and emerging talent, featuring cross-generational collaborations, unreleased music debuts, custom fashion styling, and large-scale production. While Southern California has long been home to a thriving Vietnamese-American community, V-Beyond is more than a regional cultural celebration. By bringing Vietnamese artists into a major American arena traditionally occupied by internationally recognized touring acts, the event is making a statement about V-pop’s place in the global music industry. We’ve seen international audiences embrace music beyond traditional language barriers over the past decade. From K-pop to Latin music, artists around the world have challenged the idea that mainstream success needs to come from English-language markets. Vietnamese music deserves to be part of that conversation, too. Including 31 artists from different generations also gives audiences a chance to experience the diversity of Vietnam’s contemporary music scene, rather than defining an entire country’s musical identity through one artist or genre. What makes V-Beyond particularly significant is the infrastructure behind it. Bringing together international entertainment companies, major music industry players, and Vietnamese talent demonstrates a growing investment in the genre’s global potential. For V-pop, the Honda Center showcase represents more than a concert. It’s an opportunity to introduce an entire music scene to new audiences, strengthen its international presence, and open doors for the next generation of Vietnamese artists. Vietnamese music isn’t waiting for the world to discover it. It’s bringing itself directly to the global stage.

Olympic champion and world record holder Kristof Milak of Hungary was given the chance to race in Beijing but will not be competing. November 25th, 2026  International, News, Previews & Recaps, Short Course World Championships There are some intriguing showdowns on the docket in the men’s backstroke events at the Short Course World Championships, with Hubert Kos, the world record holder in the 100 and 200 back and the defending gold medalist in the 200, headlining the field alongside Xu Jiayu and Pieter Coetze, who both lowered the 50 back world record earlier this year. The men’s 50 backstroke field is stacked with the last three world record holders all in the field. In November 2022, Kliment Kolesnikov blasted his way to a time of 22.11, breaking Florent Manaudou‘s eight-year-old mark of 22.22, which notably still stands as the World Championship Record. Kolesnikov’s record stood for nearly four years until this fall, when the mark was broken twice in just over two weeks. Pieter Coetze. Photo: Mickael Malaper/Malaper Photography South Africa’s Pieter Coetze dropped a time of 22.09 during the second leg of the 2026 World Cup circuit in Tashkent, breaking Kolesnikov’s world record. One week earlier, Russia’s Egor Kornev won the event in a World Cup Record of 22.23, with Coetze tying with another Russian, Pavel Samusenko, for the runner-up position in 22.51—a swim that lowered Coetze’s own African Record of 22.75 from 2024. Then, at the final stop of the series, Coetze won the 50 back again in 22.36, topping Samusenko (22.49) and Kornev (22.81). Samusenko had been even faster, 22.35, at the second stop when Coetze broke the world record. Kolesnikov was also a factor at the World Cup, recording times of 22.99, 22.88 and 23.03 across the three-stop circuit. Just 15 days later, China’s Xu Jiayu set a new all-time mark, firing off a time of 22.03 at the Chinese SC National Championships to lower Coetze’s world record. Kornev won’t race the 50 back at Worlds, making way for Samusenko and Kolesnikov, but another name to watch for from the World Cup is Estonian Ralf Tribuntsov, who posted back-to-back times of 22.72 and 22.96 at the last two legs of the series. Tribuntsov is the reigning SC European champion in the event, having set a national record of 22.63 in the semis before winning the final last December in 22.68. There have been a total of 10 men sub-22.8 this season, and seven of them will be in the field at Worlds. In addition to Xu, Coetze, Samusenko, Kolesnikov and Tribuntsov, we’ll also see American Adam Chaney and Frenchman Lysander Osman in the mix. Chaney won the U.S. SC World Trials in a time of 22.71, while Osman clocked 22.77 at the French Elite SC Championships. Osman is currently in his sophomore year at Kentucky, while another current NCAA swimmer who could be a factor is Miroslav Knedla, a Czech native who’s in his junior year at Indiana. Knedla won silver last year at SC Euros in a time of 22.69, and has had a strong start to the NCAA season—including clocking 23.10 in the 50 back during a SCM meet in October. The X Factor in the event could end up being Hungarian Hubert Kos, the world record holder in the 100 and 200 back. Kos owns a best time of 22.64, and has been 22.92 or faster eight different times in his career, but it remains to be seen if he can get down to the 22-low that may be required to reach the podium in Beijing. Unlike the rest of the medal contenders, he hasn’t had the SCM reps over the last few months, which could give the others an edge in a race that will be decided by such thin margins. It’s difficult to look past Coetze and Xu for a top-two spot after their world record performances in October, while Samusenko’s consistency makes him our pick to round out the podium. Kolesnikov is an intriguing name, and he’s certainly put his stamp on this event with an incredible 32 career swims sub-23, but he’s only been sub-22.7 once since 2023, so we’re picking him to end up outside the top four. Not unlike the 50, the men’s 100 backstroke features a loaded field that’s both top-heavy and has plenty of depth. And though there are 11 men lining up who have already broken 50 seconds this season, the battle for medals looks like it could come down to four, maybe five, swimmers. Headlining the start list is Hubert Kos, who, despite not racing the World Cup circuit this fall like many of his competitors, is the man to beat after breaking the world record last year in a time of 48.16. Kos is also the top returner from the 2024 SC World Championships, having one silver behind Russian Miron Lifintsev (48.76) by three one-hundredths in 48.79. The only question is whether or not Kos is rusty at all, given that we haven’t seen him racing since the European Championships in August. Pieter Coetze will be Kos’ main challenger in this event coming off sweeping it at the World Cup and earning the Triple Crown. The South African will have an extra $15,000 on the line in Beijing, as, if he wins gold in the 100 back, he’ll claim the “Double Crown” bonus for running the table across the three World Cup stops and the World Championships. Coetze, who came into the World Cup last month with a personal best time and African Record of 49.35 from 2024, brought that mark down to 49.11 in Baku, and then blasted a time of 48.21 at the second World Cup stop in Tashkent. That marked the second-fastest performance ever behind Kos’ world record. Coetze finished things off with another one of the quickest performances ever, clocking 48.40 (#4 all-time) at the final stop of the series in Astana to secure the Triple Crown. The 22-year-old is on a real hot streak, having won six medals at the Commonwealth Games in the summer, including sweeping the men’s backstroke events, prior to his dominant World Cup. Along with Coetze, the only other two men who have gone under 49 seconds this season are Pavel Samusenko and Xu Jiayu. Samusenko was consistent across the World Cup, placing 2nd to Coetze at all three stops with times of 49.24, 49.17 and 49.29. The Russian native broke 49 seconds for the first time at the 2025 Vladimir Salnikov Cup in 48.78, and then earlier this month, lowered that to 48.61 at the Russian SC Championships to rank #6 all-time in the event. He narrowly missed out on a medal at the 2024 SC World Championships, taking 4th in 49.20, just four one-hundredths back of bronze medalist Kacper Stokowski. Xu, who set the SCM world record in the 100 back at 48.88 back in 2018, went under that mark for the first time in October at the Chinese Nationals, resetting his Asian Record in 48.77. Xu has not raced at SC Worlds since 2018, when he won silver in the 100 back behind Ryan Murphy. Now 31 and the world record holder in the 50, the shorter event will clearly be his better shot at winning gold, but he could still easily crack the podium here in the 100. Behind those four, there’s a bunched up group of men between 49.5 and 50.0 this season, led by American Adam Chaney (49.50), Frenchman Lysander Osman (49.78) and Mark Nikolaev (49.79), who will be making his debut representing Australian in Beijing. However, another swimmer who needs to be watched is Thomas Ceccon, the reigning European SC champion in the 100 back who, like Kos, has not raced since the LC Euros in August. Ceccon is still the fastest man ever in the 100 back in the long course pool, but is a half-step behind that level in SCM, given that he’s yet to break the 49-second barrier. The Italian owns a best time of 49.29, set last December when he won SC Euros, and he’s been between 49.59 and 49.68 four other times, set across 2022 and 2025. Given the proximity of the 100 back and 50 fly in Beijing, it’s also possible Ceccon opts out of the 100 back. At the 2022 SC Worlds, he did not swim the 100 back, but still posted a time leading off the Italian men’s 4×100 medley relay that would’ve been 4th in the individual event. Italy’s Lorenzo Mora (49.82), Czechia’s Jan Cejka (49.84), France’s Yohann Ndoye-Brouard (49.85), Estonian Ralf Tribuntsov (49.88) and American Owen McDonald (49.96) are the other swimmers in the field who have been sub-50 this season. Canada’s Blake Tierney was 5th in the 2024 final, where he set a national record of 49.39, and he recently went 50.08 at the World Cup, so he’s another name to watch for. It’s hard to call this one between Kos and Coetze, but Kos just has an air about him, especially in short course, that makes him our pick for gold. Samusenko’s consistency gives him the nod over Xu for bronze. While there are three or four men who could realistically win gold in the 50 and 100 back at Worlds, there’s only one in the 200 back. Hubert Kos is the slam-dunk favorite, having dominated his way to gold at the 2024 edition by more than three seconds in 1:45.65, missing Mitch Larkin‘s longstanding world record by two one-hundredths. Then, during last year’s World Cup finale in Toronto, Kos roared to a time of 1:45.12 to erase Larkin’s decade-old mark of 1:45.63 by nearly half a second. Since then, Kos has re-lowered his NCAA and U.S. Open Record in the 200 back in short course yards at the NCAA Championships (1:34.13), and he produced the second-fastest swim ever in the long course event at the European Championships, clocking 1:52.30 to break his own European Record. On paper, Kos doesn’t have any real challengers in this event, though one man could make it interesting. Pieter Coetze did exactly what Kos did last year at the World Cup, sweeping the 200 back to win the Triple Crown, but it almost felt like he was doing just enough to win, and has more in the tank. Coetze broke the 50 back world record and nearly took down Kos’ 100-meter mark at the World Cup, but in the 200, he simply secured comfortable wins at each stop, culminating with a new best time of 1:48.08 in Astana—the only leg of the series where someone else went sub-1:50. After Coetze went 1:53.36 in the long course 200 back at the 2025 World Championships, nearly upsetting Kos for gold, it feels like he’s capable of something in the 1:46-1:47 range in short course, but we’ll see. He was a bit off his best, winning Commonwealth gold in 1:54.22, in the summer. Hugo Gonzalez and Destin Lasco (photo: Jack Spitser) After world #1 Gabriel Jett withdrew from the meet due to injury, Hugo Gonzalez (1:47.84) and Destin Lasco (1:47.94) are the only swimmers in the field who have been sub-1:48 this year. Gonzalez and Lasco, former teammates at Cal, could well end up being the ones battling it out for the bronze medal, as beyond Coetze’s 1:48.08, no one else in the world rankings has been under 1:49 this season. Ireland’s John Shortt should factor in the medal battle, however, as he won the 2025 SC European title in 1:47.89, setting the World Junior Record, and he was 1:49.02 earlier this month in Madrid. Russians Georgii Smirnov (1:49.17) and Dmitrii Savenko (1:49.64), Frenchman Yohann Ndoye-Brouard (1:49.31), and the Japanese duo of Daiki Yanagawa (1:49.75) and Kodai Nishiono (1:49.79) are the other men in the field who have been under 1:50 this season. France’s Mewen Tomac and Czechia’s Jan Cejka joined Shortt on the 2025 SC Euro podium, and were both finalists at the 2024 SC Worlds, so they should be factors as well. Italian Lorenzo Mora as some positive juju on his side coming in, having placed 4th at the 2021 SC Worlds, winning bronze in 2022, and then claiming silver two years ago. Although it would take some crazy circumstances for him to win gold, his consistency is remarkable and he can’t be overlooked. His teammate Thomas Ceccon is also entered in the event, and he could be a podium threat after setting a best time of 1:47.49 last year at the World Cup. Canadian Blake Tierney missed the final at the 2024 SC Worlds in 11th, but lowered his best time to 1:50.56 during the World Cup, placing 2nd to Coetze in Tashkent. He’s coming off winning silver in the LC 200 back at Pan Pacs, and looks like someone capable of going under 1:50 and cracking the final. We’re picking Coetze to win silver behind Kos, while Shortt, who is still just 19, is on the rise and gets our pick for the bronze medal. title: Xavier v. Texas A&M: Preview, matchups, and keys to the game - Banners On The Parkway
content: I’ve spilled a lot of digital ink this week explaining why I think this week is the pivotal one in Xavier’s season. The Musketeers start this two game stretch with Texas A&M and wrap it with Virginia. At the end of those two games Xavier will know how this season is going to go. They’re either good enough to play at the top level or they’re going to be left battling for, at best, table scraps. Add Banners On The Parkway as a preferred source to see more of our reporting on Google. The Musketeers come in off the back of what can only be called a really bad loss. When the game came down to winning time, which it did remarkably early, Iowa made the plays. Xavier very much did not. The Musketeers have shot the ball pretty poorly this season, but they took it to a new level by shooting 32.3% inside the arc, 37.5% outside the arc, and 69.2% (somehow an improvement) from the line. That led to an 18 point loss that, frankly, wasn’t that competitive. The Aggies, on the other hand, beat Oklahoma State, demolished Se. Louisiana, and then beat TCU on the road in their last three. They are rolling on the strength of the eighth ranked offense and 29th ranked defense in the nation. Bucky McMillan left Samford to get to Texas A&M the same season that Xavier got Coach Pitino. Since arriving he took the Aggies to the tournament last season behind Rashaun Agee doing everything and Ruben Dominguez shooting 40% from behind the arc. The good news is that Dominguez isn’t shooting nearly that well this year, the bad news is that he’s shooting badly for a new team: Xavier. Texas A&M plays fast. Fastest in the nation kind of fast. They take less than 13 seconds to get a shot up in their average possession. They do that so they can get downhill to the rim, which they do relentlessly. The Aggies have taken 183 shots at the rim, 124 above the elbow threes, and only 83 shots anywhere else on the floor. They aren’t going to waste time getting that shot up, which explains the shot selection. The Aggies get 1.23 PPS from those threes, which is good. On defense the Aggies hate nothing quite so much as trying to defensive rebound. They’ll sell out to try to get turnovers, which they generally do quite well, and dominate inside the arc. They defend behind the arc with the same general listlessness with which they offensive rebound. Make shots from deep and you’ve got a really good chance to beat these guys. Texas A&M is currently getting 41% of their minutes from the bench, though that number should probably be taken with a bit of a grain of salt since they’ve gotten a lot of minutes from deep bench guys during blowouts. No chance that happens today though, right!? #positivity Rylan Griffen is a 6’5” senior wing that has been with the Aggies the past two seasons. He’s a shooter and a really good one, connecting on 42% of his 171 three-point attempts at Texas A&M. He’s a good defender who doesn’t board or distribute much, but he’s a three-level scorer who will get them in bunches if given the opportunity. The bench big is Josh Irving; he’s a 6’11” freshman out of Pasadena. He gets 6 and 5 per game is just 13.5 minutes. He dropped 14 and 10 on Oklahoma State in a career-high 23 minutes and generally handles the glass well on both ends. He blocks a ton of shots, but he also commits a ton of fouls, especially against good competition. Jalen Reece completes what I’ve decided to call the Big Three, providing point guard help. He’s an LSU transfer who has been a bit slow out of the blocks this year, owing to foul trouble and some turnover issues. He hasn’t turned the ball over at all in their two high-major games, for whatever that’s worth, but he’s averaging 6 fouls per 40. He’s not much of a shooter, but that doesn’t stop him trying, and I think that’s brave. We might see senior guard Tyshawn Archie come off the bench chucking or Neiko Mundy get a brief look on the ball, but mostly it’s those three carrying the mail off the bench. - Can Xavier shoot? This game will functionally come down to whether Xavier can maintain Texas A&M’s scoring pace. To do that, the Musketeers will have to make some three pointers. X lost the only game so far this year where they took more threes than twos, largely because they don’t shoot the three well enough to make up for a bad night inside. They are likely to experience some real adversity inside the arc today. They need to shoot well. - Who wins the battle at the rim? X doesn’t block shots, but they are exceptionally good in defense near the rim. Teams shoot 50.4% at the rim against the Musketeers, which is an excellent number. A&M is also excellent at the rim on offense. Whoever can assert a bit of dominance there has a major edge in the game. - Is Xavier’s depth a help or hindrance? The Aggies get even more minutes from their bench than Xavier does, but they aren’t quite as balanced. Cade Phillips’ injury deprives A&M of some of that depth and Jalen Reece isn’t necessarily a value added piece. If there is a game to 10 deep, this is it. - Don’t get steamrolled: This thing is going to start fast and stay fast. In neither of the Aggies big wins have they gone on a serious run, but they are relentless. That they haven’t gone on massive run yet doesn’t mean they won’t. - Get on the offensive glass: Xavier isn’t a great offensive rebounding team, but they have the pieces to be. Mike Nwoko and Nikos Chitikoudis are both great on the glass but could be limited by foul trouble and injury, respectively. The Musketeers need someone to take advantage of the opportunities that will be readily available. - Make shots: If you’ve read this far, you probably get the idea. To win, X needs to knock down threes. If they don’t, they won’t. Xavier welcomes the MAC’s EMU Eagles to the Cintas for their second game of the season. title: Marilyn V. Dinges - Richland Source
content: North Central Ohio's Independent Local News A life well lived is measured not only in years, but in the friendships made, the lives touched, and the memories shared along the way. Marilyn lived a remarkable 100 years, finding joy in the simple pleasures of life, giving her time to others, and treasuring the family and friends who made life special. Marilyn passed away November 23, 2026, at Brethren Care in Ashland. The daughter of Detroit and Erma (Crum) Parr, Marilyn was born June 18, 1926, in Mansfield. She made her home in the Mansfield community throughout her life. Marilyn worked as a buyer for Peabody Barnes, Covert Manufacturing, and finished her career in the purchasing department at MedCentral Health System. Marilyn was a faithful member of First English Lutheran Church in Mansfield. Her church family was an important part of her life, and she enjoyed serving in several ways, including the Sarah Circle, as a communion guide, and through the church prayer chain. Her faith and willingness to serve others were reflected in her love for her church family. Marilyn also believed in giving back beyond her church. She was a member of the Daughters of the American Revolution, Women’s Auxiliary of Mansfield Hospital and RSVP (Retired Senior Volunteer Program). She especially enjoyed volunteering at The Store in Mansfield, an organization that helped provide for underprivileged children in the community. She was happy to give her time to causes that made a difference in the lives of others. When she wasn’t volunteering, Marilyn enjoyed keeping her mind busy and staying connected with the world around her. She loved a good game of euchre and enjoyed playing cards with her group of friends. An avid reader, she appreciated a good book and made a habit of reading the daily newspaper. More than anything, Marilyn treasured time spent with family and friends. Whether sharing conversation, laughter, or a simple meal, these moments were among her greatest pleasures. Reaching the age of 100 was a remarkable milestone, and Marilyn’s long life was filled with countless memories, friendships, and opportunities to make a difference. She will be remembered for her generous spirit, her community involvement, and the many simple ways she made life better for those around her. She is survived by her daughters Lynn LaFene (Tim Timar) of Huron, Nancy (Tom) Allen of Winter Springs, FL; several nieces and nephews; step grandchildren Robert (Kristina) Allen, Ryan (Emma) Allen; step great grandchildren Ellie, Leah and Luke. In addition to her parents, Marilyn was preceded in death by siblings Jane Harper, Leoma Princehorn, Robert Parr; half brother Harry Parr and her lifelong friend Doris Bechtel. Friends may call Tuesday, December 1, 2026 from 10 am to 11 am in the Finefrock Chapel of the Marion Avenue Snyder Funeral Home, where the funeral service will be held at 11 am. Burial will follow in Mansfield Cemetery. Memorial donations may be made to First English Lutheran Church or the charity of the donor’s choice. title: In Gambia v. Myanmar, the ICJ Links Statelessness to Genocide - Just Security
content:
On Nov. 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) issued its decision in The Gambia v. Myanmar. For the first time since the 1948 Genocide Convention was adopted, a court found that a State was directly responsible for committing genocide. The decision is also historic as it is the first time the ICJ has opined on the rights of stateless persons. Never before has an international court recognized that the discriminatory denial of citizenship and denationalization of a group can be a relevant factor in inferring genocidal intent. This is important as there are historic and contemporary connections between statelessness and genocide that should be recognized in order to further the goals of atrocity prevention. While the judgment is groundbreaking in this respect, as noted in the Joint Declaration of Judge Leonardo Brant and Judge ad hoc Navi Pillay, the Court could have gone further in highlighting the connection between statelessness and genocide and in considering what remedies are available to the Rohingya to ensure equal access to citizenship in Myanmar. The case was brought by The Gambia following violent actions by Myanmar against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority group primarily residing in Rakhine State. But these actions did not occur in a vacuum. The Rohingya had been subject to decades of discrimination and violence, culminating in the “clearance operations” in 2016-2017 in which hundreds of thousands were displaced, and thousands were killed or endured sexual and gender-based violence, including mass and gang rape. The Rohingya are one of the largest stateless populations in the world. While they had resided in Myanmar for generations, the Rohingya lost their right to citizenship following the passage of the 1982 Citizenship Law, which created three types of citizenship and excluded those who were not among the “national races.” As discussed by the Court in its judgment (paras. 138-139), those who might have qualified for citizenship under the new law were generally prevented from acquiring it through complex verification procedures that were discriminatorily applied against the Rohingya. The Rohingya were issued identity cards and then subsequently pressured to accept National Verification Cards, which identified the Rohingya as non-citizens. While some refused to accept them, without the National Verification Cards, the Rohingya could not access many of their basic rights. In presenting its case against Myanmar, The Gambia argued that the discriminatory laws and policies implemented by Myanmar were evidence of genocidal intent. This included Myanmar’s discriminatory denial of nationality as a means through which to deprive the Rohingya of their fundamental rights. In its written and oral pleadings, The Gambia detailed how the Rohingya had been stripped of citizenship through the passage of the 1982 Citizenship Law and prevented from accessing their rights to citizenship through the discriminatory implementation of this law. It argued how this, as a part of systemic discrimination, was designed to facilitate the Rohingya’s destruction as a group. The Gambia also situated these facts in the context of history. It highlighted how the Nuremberg Tribunal had previously found that stripping Jews of “their rights of citizenship” had “paved the way for the ‘final solution.’” As The Gambia stated during the hearing on the merits, “So too here: Myanmar’s discriminatory policies paved the way for the genocidal ‘clearance operations.’” In reviewing these facts, the Court considered Myanmar’s laws and policies on citizenship to be discriminatory. It recognized that the discriminatory denial of citizenship “contributed to the progressive erosion of the political and civil rights of the Rohingya in Rakhine State” and left the Rohingya “marginalized and particularly vulnerable.” In its assessment of factors relevant to establishing an inference of genocidal intent, the Court considered the “long-standing legislative and other forms of discrimination against the Rohingya” as one of four elements relevant to the “general context, including the perpetration of other culpable acts systematically directed against the group.” The discriminatory denial of citizenship and denationalization of the Rohingya, rendering them stateless, was a prime example of the legislative and other forms of discrimination of the Rohingya that the Court considered to have left the population vulnerable to genocide. In its submissions, The Gambia requested that, as a consequence for its breaches of the Genocide Convention, Myanmar “must offer assurances and guarantees of non-repetition by notably providing full and equal citizenship to all members of the Rohingya group who are present in Myanmar or have been displaced due to the events for which Myanmar bears responsibility under the Convention.” The Court declined this request, stating that “ordering the provision of citizenship for all members of the Rohingya group is beyond the scope of appropriate assurances and guarantees of non-repetition for acts of genocide in the circumstances before it.” In explaining its decision, however, the Court reiterated that it had “concluded that denial of citizenship for the Rohingya has been central to the overall pattern of discrimination and vulnerability that it has identified… and, as such, is a consideration in the determination of genocidal intent.” Further, it did state that Myanmar should “ensure the protection of the Rohingya against discrimination and persecution, including with respect to access to citizenship” as a restitution measure. It also stated that “additional appropriate guarantees may include, inter alia, legal and institutional reform to ensure compliance with relevant international human rights law.” However, provisions explicitly concerning citizenship were not included in the operative paragraphs of the Judgment. Judge Brant and Judge ad hoc Pillay wrote separately in a joint declaration to state that the Court should have included in the operative paragraphs an obligation for Myanmar to ensure equal access to citizenship for the Rohingya. In the words of Judge Brant and Judge ad hoc Pillay, “equal access to citizenship is the cornerstone of the protection of the Rohingya’s rights under the Genocide Convention and the first guarantee against the commission of genocide” (emphasis added). Judge Brant and Judge ad hoc Pillay also emphasized what they viewed as a causal connection between the denial of citizenship and genocide. As they stated, “the denial of citizenship leads to discriminatory measures (such as restrictions on employment, education and freedom of movement), which in turn lead to marginalization, from which ensues greater vulnerability.” They also emphasized the connection between access to citizenship and atrocity prevention. As the present case has demonstrated, the denial of citizenship can facilitate systematic violations of human rights that, in their most extreme form, amount to genocide. To the extent that access to citizenship is essential to the effective enjoyment and exercise of human rights for the Rohingya, it also serves as a safeguard against violations of those rights and thereby contributes to the prevention of genocide. In their view, Myanmar’s obligation to ensure equal access to citizenship is clear in reading the Judgment as a whole, if not in reading the operative paragraphs in isolation. The reason the Court may have declined to grant the Gambia’s request to provide “full and equal citizenship to all members of the Rohingya group” and rather focused on access to citizenship as a measure of restitution to “ensure the protection of the Rohingya from discrimination and persecution” is that “full and equal citizenship [for] all members of the Rohingya group” is not reflective of Myanmar’s obligations under international law and goes beyond what international law requires. First, although it may seem subtle, nationality and citizenship are distinct concepts. International law governs nationality, which is the individual’s relationship with the State. While these terms are often used interchangeably, there are important distinctions, particularly in the context of Myanmar’s 1982 Citizenship Law, which creates several tiers of citizenship. As The Gambia argued in its written pleadings, the Rohingya were only eligible for “associate” or “naturalized” citizenship under the 1982 Law, which The Gambia described as an “inferior status” of citizenship due to lesser access to rights. While the principles of equality and non-discrimination are foundational to international human rights law, international law does not generally prohibit tiers of citizenship, nor does it clearly circumscribe that different citizenship statuses may come with different access to rights. As the definition of a stateless person under international law is “a person who is not considered a national by any State under the operation of its law,” a person could even be a national, but not a citizen, of a state and not be stateless. (For example, in the United States, persons born in American Samoa are nationals, but not citizens of the United States and naturalized citizens are not eligible to be president.) So, it is not clear that – absent requiring Myanmar to apply its citizenship law in a non-discriminatory way – international law would require Myanmar to grant all members of the Rohingya group a specific tier of citizenship as any tier would restore their right to a nationality and address their statelessness. Under international law, an individual’s right to a nationality is, unfortunately, not absolute. And international law does not require States to guarantee to every person within its territory a nationality. As stated by the Court in the Nottebohm decision, “it is for every sovereign State, to settle by its own legislation the rules relating to the acquisition of its nationality, and to confer that nationality by naturalization granted by its own organs in accordance with that legislation.” While international law has continued to evolve to narrow the circumstances under which a State may withdraw its nationality, particularly when done on discriminatory grounds or when it results in statelessness, States still retain a large amount of discretion in this area. While Myanmar is not a state party to either the 1954 Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons or the 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness, it is a party to the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) and the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women, both of which contain provisions on acquisition of nationality. The Gambia would have done well to have framed the issue of citizenship stripping and its request for assurances and non-repetition in terms of the right to a nationality and international law on statelessness, particularly where Myanmar has undertaken binding obligations concerning a right to a nationality or there are norms that are grounded in and reflective of customary international law. In its Memorial, The Gambia submitted “that any assurance and guarantee of non-repetition must aim at the full legal recognition and protection of the members of the Rohingya group under Myanmar’s laws.” In order to give effect to the request that the Rohingya group be given full legal recognition, the Gambia could have included a request that Myanmar register all Rohingya children born in Myanmar immediately after birth, as reflective of Myanmar’s obligation under Article 7 of the CRC. Given that The Gambia built some of its case on the fact that Myanmar refused to register or acknowledge Rohingya births, this could have been a powerful complement to a request for assurance and guarantee of non-repetition concerning citizenship – especially as birth registration is often critical for a person’s full legal recognition and essential for the prevention of statelessness. Article 7 of the CRC also reflects this connection, stating that every child shall have “the right to acquire a nationality.” It provides that States Parties, such as Myanmar, shall ensure the implementation of the rights, “in particular where the child would otherwise be stateless.” The failure to make this connection between Myanmar’s refusal to register Rohingya births, their statelessness and thus vulnerability to genocide in its submissions was a missed opportunity. The Court was unlikely to order assurances and guarantees of non-repetition that exceed a State’s obligations under the statelessness conventions, particularly as Myanmar is not a state party. However, The Gambia could have framed its request in terms of Myanmar providing assurances that the Rohingya would not be arbitrarily deprived of their nationality. Under the 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness, a State “may not deprive any person or group of persons of their nationality on racial, ethnic, religious or political grounds.” As noted by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, States’ obligations to adhere to the principle of non-discrimination under customary international law complement Article 9 of the 1961 Convention, which is important when considering Myanmar’s obligations. So, while there are some limited circumstances in which a State may deprive a person of their nationality, under the Convention, “the deprivation of nationality that would result in statelessness is strictly circumscribed.” Furthermore, there is a prohibition on the arbitrary deprivation of nationality, which includes instances “where a State arbitrarily precludes a person or group from obtaining or retaining a nationality (e.g., on discriminatory grounds).” The Joint Declaration by Judge Brant and Judge ad hoc Pillay strikes the right balance of stressing non-discrimination in that the Court should have ordered “equal access to citizenship,” (emphasis in the original) in the operative paragraphs rather than The Gambia’s more absolutist framing. It is perhaps unfortunate that a more balanced request that also included more robust protections against statelessness, such as requiring birth registration, wasn’t submitted to the Court. The Court might have found a way forward that more closely hewed to the perspective presented in the Joint Declaration with explicit reference to Myanmar’s obligation to ensure equal access to citizenship in the operative paragraphs. Even with the deficiencies in how the remedies were requested and granted, the Court did elaborate in the Judgment that as a part of the ordered restitution to “ensure the protection of the Rohingya from discrimination and persecution,” this should include “access to citizenship.” This decision should also put States on notice that the discriminatory denial of a nationality and denationalization of a group can be a relevant factor in inferring genocidal intent. It is also important context for identifying situations in which discriminatory citizenship laws are a key part of a broader pattern of discrimination and violence and raise concerns about the potential for atrocity crimes or even genocide. This case should also bring awareness to the role that statelessness plays in genocide. Even when the denial of a nationality occurs after much of the violence has ceased, it can serve as a permanent exclusion from the political community and a continuation of the genocidal process. In human rights terms, the “denial of citizenship” or the “stripping of citizenship” or the “denationalization” of the Rohingya in the lead up to the genocide all amount to a denial of the right to a nationality. As I have written elsewhere, the protection of a right to a nationality under international law is far too weak in comparison to its role in ensuring universal access to human rights. The Court took an important step in strengthening the right to a nationality in finding that the discriminatory denial of citizenship was a relevant, if not a central, factor in finding the existence of genocidal intent. It unfortunately stopped short of explicitly ensuring the Rohingya’s access to this right, which may prove to be regrettable. Even so, one can hope that this decision will help to illuminate the role of the right to a nationality in preventing the most serious violations of human rights, including genocide. Melissa Stewart (Bluesky - LinkedIn) is an Associate Professor of Law at the University of Connecticut, where she holds joint appointments at the School of Law and the Gladstein Family Human Rights Institute. title: The Gambia v. Myanmar and the Duty to Prevent Genocide - Opinio Juris
content: In association with the International Commission of Jurists [Jinan Bastaki is Associate Professor of Legal Studies at New York University, Abu Dhabi and a contributing editor at Opinio Juris.] The International Court of Justice’s recent judgment in The Gambia v. Myanmar (19 November 2026) provides an important clarification of the obligations of States under the Genocide Convention, particularly the obligation to prevent genocide. In the earlier 2007 Bosnia v. Serbia case, the Court explained that the obligation to prevent genocide is triggered by the existence of a serious risk (Bosnia v. Serbia, para. 432). That said, the Court also stated that “if neither genocide nor any of the other acts listed in Article III of the Convention are ultimately carried out, then a State that omitted to act when it could have done so cannot be held responsible a posteriori” (para. 431). Hence, the Court stuck to Serbia’s responsibility under the Convention in relation to Srebrenica, since the ICTY had already found that genocide had been committed. This creates somewhat of a contradiction: the purpose of the obligation to prevent is to ensure, as far as possible, that a genocide does not take place, but in order ascertain whether a state has abided by that obligation, there must have been a determination that genocide has occurred. The ICJ resolved this contradiction in The Gambia v. Myanmar. The Court re-affirmed that that the trigger for the obligation to prevent was the existence of a serious risk, and it also added that it is the serious risk itself and not a definitive judicial determination that genocide has occurred that was the source of the obligation. An obligation whose purpose is prevention cannot reasonably be understood to arise only after the crime it is intended to prevent has been judicially established. As the DRC stated, and was quoted by the Court in its judgment, “Conditioning the breach of the obligation to prevent on the prior establishment of a violation of Article III would likely lead to results that are manifestly absurd and unreasonable, and be contrary to the object and purpose of the Convention.” (The Gambia v. Myanmar, para. 475, emphasis added). The Court itself then emphasized that a state should not be allowed to “remain idle and gamble” (para. 487). This matters particularly for States that continue to justify their conduct (or their inaction) on the basis that no international court has definitively found Israel to have committed genocide. The Genocide Convention does not permit States to treat the absence of a final judgment as a reason to remain passive or just do the bare minimum (e.g. the way certain states suspended some weapons licenses), since the duty to prevent is much more comprehensive than the duty not to be complicit. This finding is also relevant to the ongoing proceedings in Nicaragua v. Germany, where Nicaragua alleges, inter alia, that Germany has failed to fulfil its obligations under the Genocide Convention through its military and other forms of assistance to Israel. The Gambia v. Myanmar: The Obligation of Due Diligence and Reaffirming Third-state Responsibility In addressing the obligation to prevent genocide, the Court reiterated that the duty arises when a State knows, or should normally know, of a serious risk of genocide (The Gambia v. Myanmar, para. 478). The Court went further in clarifying the relationship between the duty to prevent and the actual commission of genocide. It expressly stated that international responsibility for breach of the obligation to prevent genocide is not conditioned on a finding that genocide has occurred (para. 487). The Court considered Myanmar’s responsibility for failing to prevent acts committed by civilians participating alongside its security forces during the 2017 clearance operations. While the Court could not conclusively determine whether those civilians themselves possessed genocidal intent (para. 486), it nevertheless concluded that their participation posed a serious risk of genocide, of which Myanmar should normally have been aware (para. 485). Myanmar had means available to it that might have contributed to preventing those acts and failed to use them (paras. 485-488). It was therefore found to have violated its obligation to prevent genocide under Article I (para. 488). In his dissenting opinion, Judge Nolte argued that the Court had departed from its earlier jurisprudence by not requiring the duty to prevent to be linked to a genocide that has actually taken place (for e.g. in Bosnia v. Serbia as mentioned above, and then in Croatia v. Serbia, no genocide was determined and therefore there was no failure to prevent). He stated that: By decoupling the breach of that duty from the actual occurrence of genocide, the Court is announcing that the legal duty to prevent genocide has far wider-ranging implications than the Court had indicated beforehand. Indeed, from now on, every State must expect to be held responsible, including before this Court, for not acting diligently enough to prevent a genocide which has not occurred. (Judge Nolte, Dissenting Opinion, para. 79) The other judges addressed this head-on, in particular Judges Cleveland and Judge Ad Hoc Kress in their joint separate opinion, as well as Judge Tladi in his separate declaration. Judge Cleveland and Judge Ad Hoc Kress stated that “it is more coherent to consider, as one commentator has put it, that ‘the “wrong” here is … doing nothing in the face of imminent genocide’” (para. 8). They showed that the Court’s reasoning in Bosnia v. Serbia was internally inconsistent, since it contradicted the object and purpose of the treaty, which explicitly includes the prevention of genocide. Hence, the “relevant wrong then consists of a failure to employ all reasonable means to eliminate or at least reduce the risk — irrespective of what follows” (para. 12). Indeed, while Judge Ad Hoc Kress disputed that Myanmar acted with genocidal intent, he nevertheless saw that that “does not by itself preclude a finding that Myanmar violated its obligation to prevent the commission of genocide by individuals acting alongside its security forces” (Judge Ad Hoc Kress, separate opinion, para. 144) The obligation to prevent, as Judge Ad Hoc Hmoud emphasized, “has a ‘separate legal existence of its own’,” (Judge Ad Hoc Hmoud, separate opinion, para. 33). Judge Tladi further clarified the internal inconsistency in Bosnia v. Serbia and Croatia v. Serbia, stating that “The ordinary meaning of the words “to prevent” is to take action before genocide occurs since genocide that has already been committed cannot be prevented,” (para. 34). Indeed, states’ obligation to prevent may never be triggered if the prerequisite is the actual determination by a court that genocide had occurred, especially since the “jurisdiction of international courts is dependent on the consent of States”, (para.35). This is consistent with other preventative obligations in international law such the duty to prevent harm to the environment and the duty of States to ensure respect for the rules of international humanitarian law under Common Article 1 of the Geneva Conventions (para. 37). This confirms that States cannot conflate the legal determination of genocide with the separate assessment of whether they have fulfilled their preventive obligations. The Court found a breach of the obligation to prevent on the basis of a serious risk, without conclusively determining the genocidal intent of the civilians whose conduct was at issue. The preventive obligation would be rendered largely meaningless if States were required to await a final determination of genocide before acting. There are two cases at the ICJ in which these obligations become particularly relevant: South Africa v. Israel and Nicaragua v. Germany. For the former, the implications for States in denial about their obligations vis-a-vis Israel are considerable, since the risk has been established not only the Court but by the increasing evidence illustrated by independent commissions and NGOs. Nicaragua v. Germany directly concerns Germany’s alleged failure to prevent genocide, including through its provision of military assistance and more broadly its special relationship with Israel. In its request for provisional measures, Nicaragua argued that Germany was continuing to support Israel despite the risk that such assistance would facilitate violations of the Genocide Convention and other rules of international law. On 30 April 2024, the ICJ declined to indicate provisional measures, which I have argued elsewhere to be an avoidance of third-state responsibility. That said, the Court did not absolve Germany or other States of their substantive obligations under the Genocide Convention. The Court expressly recalled the obligations of States concerning arms transfers and the risk that arms might be used to violate the Genocide Convention and international humanitarian law (Nicaragua v. Germany, para. 24). Moreover, as Judge Cleveland emphasized in her declaration, the obligation to prevent genocide under Article I is distinct from the prohibition on complicity under Article III(e). The former imposes positive obligations to act; it is not limited to refraining from knowingly facilitating genocide. A State may breach its preventive obligation through its failure to take reasonably available measures once it knows, or should know, of a serious risk (Declaration of Judge Cleveland, paras. 4-5). The Court’s reasoning in The Gambia v. Myanmar reinforces this distinction. The obligation to prevent is autonomous and prospective. It does not depend upon the eventual success of the preventive measures taken, nor upon a final judicial finding that genocide has occurred. The relevant question is whether a State has used all reasonably available means, in light of the risk and its capacity to influence. While there is not yet a determination of genocide, the ICJ’s provisional measures orders in South Africa v. Israel recognized the plausibility of rights under the Genocide Convention and the risk of irreparable harm to those rights. The Court repeatedly emphasized the grave humanitarian conditions and the need for measures to protect the Palestinian population. Further, in September 2025, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry concluded that “the State of Israel bears responsibility for the failure to prevent genocide, the commission of genocide and the failure to punish genocide against the Palestinians in the Gaza Strip,” (para. 255). In The Gambia v. Myanmar, the Court explained the extent to which it would rely on third-party fact-finding, considering “the independence and qualifications of the author, the methodology used in the preparation of the evidence, and the comprehensive nature and overall quality of the evidence,” (para. 97). Moreover, it stated that, “Where such evidence is corroborated by other evidence, the Court will accord greater weight to it,” (para. 100). At the very least, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry further underscores the seriousness of the risk, particularly as it is corroborated by numerous reports of human rights organizations, and the reports of the UN Special Rapporteur on the Situation of Human Rights in the Palestinian Territories. Capacity to Influence and the Means Available to States Against this backdrop, the fact that States seem to be waiting until the ICJ conclusively determines whether Israel has committed genocide contradicts the Convention’s preventive purpose. The obligation is designed to operate before certainty. As I previously argued in line with Bosnia v. Serbia, the scope of the obligation must be understood in light of the means States possess to influence those committing, or at risk of committing, genocide. The strength of political, military, financial, and other relationships matters in assessing capacity to influence (see Bosnia v. Serbia, paras. 430-431, 434). The obligation is a positive obligation to act, and to act comprehensively, not just symbolically. Germany, for example, has argued that the Genocide Convention requires a strict standard of proof regarding specific genocidal intent (dolus specialis) and that provisional measures do not establish that genocide is occurring. While it suspended certain weapons that may be used in Gaza (in August of 2025), it ignored more comprehensive measures. The EU, too, remains in a posture of “reviewing” rather than suspending the EU-Israel Association Agreement, and sanctions by States have been confined to those involved in settlement activities or individual Israelis, rather than Israel itself. Most states have undertaken modest measures, if any at all. The existence of extensive reporting, findings by UN bodies, provisional measures issued by the ICJ, and continued warnings concerning the situation in Gaza are all relevant to whether States knew, or should normally have known, of that risk. The obligation to prevent genocide is assessed in concreto. States must therefore evaluate the means available to them and employ those means as far as circumstances permit. The obligation is not confined to arms transfers, although arms transfers are an obvious and important means of influence. States must consider all available measures, including the suspension of military assistance, diplomatic pressure, economic measures, and cooperation through international organizations. States cannot treat grave violations of international law as matters for a Court to resolve while continuing relationships that sustain the situation. The Gambia v. Myanmar judgment brings consistency to the obligation: The obligation to prevent genocide is one of due diligence, and a breach may be established independently of a definitive finding that genocide occurred.
